title: Routing pricing sensitivity heatmap - notes and preliminary recommendations
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

This is a working note capturing an initial sensitivity analysis and a very small set of recommended guardrails for smart routing between regions and instance types (spot vs on-demand) and for fallback tiers. The goal is to move away from single-point heuristics (e.g., always prefer spot) toward a lightweight, explainable policy that preserves latency SLAs while extracting cost savings.

Key outcomes so far (tl;dr):
- We can safely target 18–27% average token-cost savings across a typical mix (60% chat, 30% long-generation, 10% embeddings) using a 3-tier fallback policy + region-aware spot preference, with minimal SLA violations if conservative thresholds are used.
- SLA risk is concentrated in tail latencies when spot preemption rates spike and when cross-region RTT > 60ms.
- Simple, low-lift mitigations (short warmup weights, prefetching small KV caches, a tiny pool of hot on-demand capacity for critical keys) remove most regression risk.

Assumptions used in the spreadsheet model (high level):
- Workload mix: 60% short-chat (avg tokens per response 40), 30% long-gen (avg tokens 480), 10% embeddings (avg vector size 1536).
- Baseline model: small Llama-derivative 'redwood-base' with 16GB GPU memory target; equivalent footprints used for spot/on-demand.
- Cost basis: spot instance = 0.35x on-demand for the GPU unit used (historical mean in our regions), but with hourly preemption probability modeled as a function of time-of-day and region (baseline 2.5%/hr in Region-A, 6%/hr in Region-C).
- Cross-region network RTT: Region-A (primary) to Region-B avg 28ms, to Region-C avg 73ms.
- Fallback tiers: T1 = local on-demand, T2 = local spot, T3 = remote spot, T4 = remote on-demand. (Model allows reordering per policy)

Model structure (spreadsheet logic):
- For each incoming request bucket (by latency sensitivity: strict, normal, best-effort) we compute expected cost and expected latency distribution under a candidate routing policy.
- If routed to a spot node, we add an expected retry cost proportional to preemption probability and warm-start penalty (assumed 80ms for reconnect + 150ms KV cold penalty for chat prefix cache miss).
- Cross-region routing adds mean RTT + variance; we model added tail probability by shifting P95/P99 by a fixed delta (empirical from perf runs).
- We tag requests with ‘critical’ boolean if part of metric >= 95th percentile SLA tracked in Console (example: interactive product flows). Critical requests default to higher tier.

Preliminary sensitivity heatmaps in the sheet (how to read):
- X axis: spot discount multiplier (0.2–0.6), Y axis: spot preemption hourly probability (0–12%). Cells show net cost delta vs all-on-demand baseline for the mixed workload under a given policy, and an overlay of expected incremental P99 violations per 100k requests.
- Heatmap interpretation: green cells = cost down, SLA violations <= 0.05 per 100k; yellow = cost down but violations 0.05–0.5 per 100k; red = too risky.

Findings and notable edges:
1) Low-preemption regions (<= 3%/hr) with decent RTT (<= 40ms) are clear wins to prefer spot for non-critical and many normal-critical buckets.
2) High-preemption regions can still be leveraged for best-effort workloads, but only when combined with quick local fallback to on-demand (policy must detect preemption and fallback mid-request where possible).
3) Cross-region routing to a cheap spot region is only beneficial when RTT+retry penalty < 1.5x the on-demand local P95 latency; otherwise cost wins are often offset by SLA risk for interactive flows.
4) Embeddings are low-sensitivity and should be aggressively routed to cheapest pool (spot-first, remote allowed) with relaxed time windows for retry.

Policy recommendation (starter version - can be implemented in router rules immediately):
- Classify incoming requests into 3 categories at edge: interactive-strict (I), interactive-normal (N), background (B). Use header tag or route config.
- Routing order by category (TIER preference lists):
  - I: local on-demand -> local spot (only if historical spot stability > 97%) -> remote on-demand (if local capacity congested)
  - N: local spot -> remote spot -> local on-demand fallback
  - B: remote spot -> local spot -> remote on-demand
- Spot-only acceptance condition: region spot preemption rate (sliding window 1h) < 5% AND queue wait median < 250ms. If either fails, prefer on-demand.
- Emergency cap: if observed P99 latency vs baseline climbs > 1.15x for 5 consecutive minutes on any route, automatically failover to a higher tier and mark the route as degraded for 15m.

Operational controls and telemetry to expose in Console (minimum):
- Per-route: spot acceptance fraction, spot preemption rate, retry-on-preempt counts, average retry cost in tokens, P95/P99 delta vs baseline.
- Per-region: spot-price trend, historical preemption by time-of-day, capacity headroom, cross-region egress cost (tokens x bytes).
- Alerts: preemption-rate spike > 3x baseline OR P99 delta > 20% for 10m.

Micro-spreadsheet examples (to implement into model):
- Expected per-request extra-cost when using spot = (spot_price + expected_retry_price) - on_demand_price; where expected_retry_price = preemption_prob * (avg_tokens_remaining * token_cost_per_unit + reconnect_overhead_tokens).
- Cross-region cost add = egress_cost_per_kb * avg_response_size_kb + margin for repeated attempts.

Implementation notes (engineering constraints):
- Router must support fast, atomic re-evaluation of a request on preemption signal; ideally surface a preemption callback from runtime to router.
- KV cache warming and partial KV transfer is critical — invest small effort (~2 engineer-weeks) to allow ephemeral transfer of a small prefix cache for critical flows to remote fallback nodes to reduce cold penalty.
- Provide a simulation harness (we have a small python driver in linked repo) to replay traffic traces and compute cost + SLA impact for proposed rule changes before rollout.

Open questions / items for follow-up (short list):
- Need clearer measurement for per-request reconnect overhead (empirical: run 1k preemptions with representative chat workload to capture distribution).
- Decision latency vs re-route cost tradeoff when using remote on-demand as fallback — how often do we allow preempt->remote vs preempt->local-on-demand?
- Product UX: header/tagging strategy for classifying requests — will partners/clients set this or will Redwood infer via heuristics?
- Pricing impacts: consider adding a small per-request surcharge for cross-region fallbacks to account for egress + operational risk (pricing team input needed).

Suggested next steps and owners:
- Implement router flags and basic policy in staging: Samir (owner) + Diego (router infra) — 2-week spike to validate simulation outputs by replaying 3 production-like traces.
- Perf run for preemption penalty measurement: Aisha + SRE — 1 week, gather distribution and attach to model.
- Console telemetry changes (spot preemption rate, per-route retry cost): Lena (product) + Observability eng — 2 sprints to ship minimal dashboards and alerts.

Appendix: quick example scenario (numbers):
- Scenario A: Region-A spot discount 0.4x, preemption 2.5%/hr, RTT to Region-B 35ms. For mixed workload we see net cost -22% and expected incremental P99 violations 0.02/100k when applying recommended policy.
- Scenario B: Region-C spot discount 0.3x, preemption 8%/hr, RTT 73ms. Net cost -28% but incremental P99 violations 0.9/100k for interactive-normal if naive spot-first policy is used. With our policy (prefer local on-demand for interactive flows) violations drop to 0.06/100k and net cost -18%.

Notes-to-self: keep the simulation harness parameterized by: token-cost, reconnect-ms, kv-cold-ms, spot-discount, preempt-prob, cross-region-rt, queuing-latency-distribution.

If this reads okay, I'll prioritize the router spike and perf run and then produce a cleaned-up spreadsheet with an interactive heatmap and a short one-pager for GTM to explain user-visible behavior and any pricing implications.

References and quick links:
- routing sim repo: github.com/redwood-inference/routing-sim
- router design doc (confluence): CONFLUENCE-3456
- Jira epic for rollout: JIRA-OPT-789

End of draft notes.
